title: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The surface to which the branches of the antler tend to be confined is a more or less spheroidal, or occasionally an ellipsoidal one; and furthermore, when we inspect any well-developed pair of antlers, such as those of a red deer, a sambur or a wapiti, we have no difficulty in seeing that the two antlers make up between them _a single surface_

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “Deer antlers”. Scope: antlers of deer and elk (Cervidae)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The assertion has a direct 3D geometric decision criterion. Public museum models and images should support a broad, feasible test across the named deer groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit a single smooth spheroid or ellipsoid to the 3D branch centerlines and tine tips of paired antlers, comparing residuals with separate surfaces and unconstrained branching models. Consistently small residuals and bilateral continuity support the claim; strongly noncoplanar or multi-surface arrangements refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A tolerance for being 'confined' to one surface must be prespecified.

Damage and annual age affect tine completeness.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.68
data existence: 0.78
discriminating power: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fitting tine tips to one mirror-symmetric curved surface is a direct test, and enough antlered skulls are publicly scanned to try it on red deer, wapiti, and similar species. That is the comparison Thompson invites, but it is not yet a family-wide sample, and shed antlers cannot test the paired surface. The analysis itself is a short geometric exercise once paired meshes are chosen.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place landmarks on tine tips of paired antlers and fit a single ellipsoid or spheroid, allowing mirror symmetry across the midline. The claim is supported if one surface accounts for both antlers within a small residual and the tips lie on a continuous curve; systematically separate surfaces for left and right, or residuals that grow with tine length, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Open 3D coverage is good for a few deer species and poor for the rest of Cervidae.

Many scans are of skulls after the antlers were shed, or of a single antler.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.5
